subject: Post-demo: token-ceiling implications and latency next steps

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>

Subject: Post-demo: token-ceiling implications and latency next steps

Hi Rajiv / Anika —

Thanks again for taking the demo today. Quick recap while the discussion is fresh and a proposed set of next steps so we can scope a focused perf run.

Key points we heard from FinQuest in the call:
- Target user experience: occasional long answers (up to ~800 tokens output) paired with long context (avg input ~900 tokens).
- User-facing SLOs: first-token streaming latency target ~500ms (p50), end-to-end p95 target ~1.2s for long flows. For short Q&A paths (<512 tokens total) target p95 <=250ms.
- Expected steady-state concurrency: ~120 concurrent active sessions during peak; expected sustained QPS ~40 requests/s with burst up to 120 req/s.

Areas we discussed that materially affect latency/cost:
- Total token budget (input + output) drives attention compute; going above ~1k tokens moves us into a different kernel/attention regime and increases per-request latency nonlinearly.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: streaming helps perceived latency for first token but can increase overall resource usage when combined with large outputs.
- Caching/KV-warmup: many of your flows reuse a shared system prompt; prefix caching will reduce cost/latency on subsequent requests.

Immediate asks from our side to size a perf test:
1) Share representative sample payloads (anonymized) covering short, medium, long flows (attach as sample_payloads.json).
2) Confirm % of traffic that requires streaming first-token vs batch-only responses.
3) Approve a controlled canary perf run on a dedicated pool (we recommend a 2h window).

Attachments: sample_payloads.json, expected_qps.csv (placeholder we used in the call).

I’ll loop Marissa and Laura in to propose concrete perf scenarios and estimated latencies across hosted vs dedicated.

Best,
Rishi

Rishi Malhotra

Thanks Rishi — good writeup. A few clarifications from our side:

- Representative sizes: most conversational turns are ~80-160 tokens, but we have an advanced search flow that sends ~700-1,000 token contexts and expects ~600-900 token outputs (so total can be 1.3k-1.9k tokens).
- Streaming requirement: for long answers we need the first token to begin streaming within ~500ms p50 to avoid a perceived stall. End-to-end p95 of 1.2s is aggressive but achievable if we get dedicated capacity or aggressive quantization.
- Traffic shape: steady 40 req/s across the cluster with spikes up to 120 req/s (bursts last ~10-15 minutes).

We can provide anonymized payloads; I’ll drop them in the attachment. Also happy to authorize a 2-hour canary on a dedicated pool as long as we have a pre-approved rollback and monitoring hook.

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Date: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 08:05:00 -0800
Subject: RE: Post-demo: token-ceiling implications and latency next steps (technical sketch)

Rajiv — thanks for the samples and the traffic profile. I did a quick pass with conservative model estimates and pulled together a short technical sketch (see attachment: redwood_perf_estimate.xlsx). Key takeaways below.

Summary of latency drivers
- Input length impact: attention is ~O(n^2) in the worst case for cross-attention-like ops; practically the kernel changes around the 1k token total mark (input+output). Requests <1k tokens follow the optimized fastpath and tend to be ~0.15–0.4s on hosted (p95 varies by model), while >1k can see a 2–3x increase depending on batching.
- Generation per-token cost: for our gpt-large-class variants we typically observe ~0.6–1.2 ms/token generation on balanced GPUs (varies by quantization). So 800 tokens output adds ~480–960 ms of pure generation time.
- Streaming first-token latency: dominated by model startup/KV fetch. With prefix caching warm, first-token can be <200–300ms on dedicated pools; hosted cold paths can be 400–700ms.

Concrete scenarios (based on your samples)
- Short flow (total 450 tokens): estimated hosted p95 ~180–260ms; dedicated p95 ~80–120ms.
- Long flow (1.7k tokens): estimated hosted p95 ~1.6–2.3s; dedicated p95 ~0.8–1.1s (with prefix cache enabled).

Recommendations to hit your SLOs
1) Dedicated pool for peak traffic windows (keeps p95 deterministic).
2) Enable prefix/KV caching for repeated system prompts; we’ll provide a config snippet.
3) Consider int8 quantization for the long-answer model variant (saves ~30–45% per-token latency in practice).
4) If streaming perceived latency is the highest priority, implement a small first-token prompt that triggers a fast-path (send a trimmed system prompt + short prefix) — we can help craft that safely.

Next steps I propose
- Rishi: schedule the 2-hour canary window (suggest Wed 11/25 10:00–12:00 PT).
- Rajiv: confirm anonymized payloads uploaded to the shared folder and whether we can run synthetic burst tests up to 120 req/s.
- Laura/CS: define monitoring hooks (token/cost dashboards + p95 latency on first-token and end-to-end).

Attachments: redwood_perf_estimate.xlsx (spreadsheet with scenario calc), small config snippet included on sheet 2.

Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
